newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Peace crisis hits fledgling Palestinian stock market.
newsitem.headline: Peace crisis hits fledgling Palestinian stock market.

text.p: The month-old crisis in Middle East peacemaking has lowered the expectations of investors in a nascent Palestinian stock exchange, officials said on Tuesday.

Safwan Bataina, general manager of the Palestine Securities Exchange (PSE), said the volume of trade has multiplied since the Nablus exchange was launched in February but the pace has not met their forecast.
"When we started trading, the peace process was moving," Bataina told Reuters. "But there has been a decisive change in the expectations of investors, brokers and traders," he said.
Israeli-Palestinian peace moves have been frozen since March 18 when Israel sent bulldozers to begin work on a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.
The settlement building ignited a wave of Palestinian protests and a bombing in which three Israeli women were killed.

Israel responded by closing off its borders with the West Bank and Gaza Strip for more than three weeks, making it impossible for most Palestinians to travel between the two areas and to reach Israel for work.

"Investors' expectations over the past month have decidedly turned negative for the first time since the Madrid (peace) conference," Bataina said, referring to the 1991 conference which launched Israeli-Arab peace talks.

Traders said more than 300,000 shares worth $300,000 were traded during Tuesday's weekly session, up from about 50,000 shares traded last week. Traders had expected the volume by now to reach about one million shares a week.
The fully electronic bourse was launched in February after Israel handed most of the West Bank town of Hebron to Palestinian self-rule.
Bataina said a two-month introductory period, during which no data is released and price movements are limited, would be extended by at least two months.

"It is not as good as we expected. But given the political situation, it is not bad at all," said Jamal Aladdin, general manager of the Jordan and Palestine Financial Investment Company, one of four brokerage firms registered with the exchange.
Aladdin said that foreign businessmen were still making enquiries about investment prospects, including the manager of a Swiss bank which administers investment protfolios.
"In spite of all the bad conditions, we are still getting orders to buy and sell shares and this shows that Palestinians can look at events objectively," he said.
